sentences.text: The genus name Kairuku comes from Māori words meaning 'food' and 'to dive', while the species name waewaeroa translates to 'long legs'.
K. grebneffi stood 1.28 meters tall and possessed the longest humerus bone of any penguin known from fossils or living species, featuring a longer bill and more slender body than modern relatives.
Relative to its size, this species had flippers that were longer and likely more flexible than those of extant penguin species, whereas K. waewaeroa could reach a height of 1.38 meters.
K. grebneffi possesses the longest humerus bone of any penguin known from either the fossil record or living species.
Relative to its body size, K. grebneffi had flippers that were longer and likely more flexible than those of extant penguin species.
Kairuku fossils date to 27 million years ago and were found in the Kokoamu Greensand Formation of New Zealand, though the first bones were discovered in 1977 by Ewan Fordyce before being identified.

In February 2012, a team led by Fordyce and Daniel Ksepka reconstructed a K. grebneffi skeleton using specimens from the Kokoamu Greensand, while the holotype was collected in 1991 from the Waipati stream drainage area.
Fossils of K. waewaeroa, known as the Kawhia giant penguin, were found in Kawhia Harbour on New Zealand's North Island.
Predators of K. grebneffi likely included sharks and Squalodons.
Kairuku was historically classified under the genus Palaeeudyptes, but the genus Kairuku was described by Ksepka, Fordyce, Ando & Jones in 2012.
K. grebneffi lived in what is now New Zealand during the late Oligocene, roughly 25 to 27 million years ago, when the area consisted mostly of ocean with a few isolated islands.
Researchers believe that rock outcrops provided safe breeding grounds and access to rich food resources for K. grebneffi.
